summary: On September 15, 2023, the Springdale city council approved sweeping tax revisions: a tiered property tax, a sales tax increase from 7.5% to 8%, and a local income tax credit for low earners. The note covers the intended benefits for low-income residents, the concerns of residents and small businesses, and the council's pledge to run workshops and revisit the structure in two years.
one_line: Springdale's city council approved a tiered property tax, an 8% sales tax and an income tax credit, prompting mixed reactions from residents and businesses.
key_facts: The Springdale city council voted on September 15, 2023 to approve sweeping tax amendments.
The amendments were spearheaded by Councilwoman Elizabeth Torres and her committee.
A tiered property tax system segments property taxes by assessed property value to ease the burden on owners of less-valued homes.
The sales tax rises from 7.5% to 8%; Councilman James O'Reilly says this will bolster revenue for infrastructure projects and community services.
A local income tax credit with a sliding scale based on annual earnings is meant to help people below an income threshold, though specifics are not yet fully outlined.
Property tax bills are expected to fall for homes valued at less than $250,000.
Amelia Sanchez, a single mother of three working two part-time jobs, said the city's growth 'can't be on the backs of those who are already struggling.'
Local businessman Richard Kemp supports the changes, citing the long-term benefits of investing in infrastructure and services.
Lily Chen, who runs a local bakery, worries the sales tax increase will reduce discretionary spending and her daily sales.
Larger businesses may benefit from improved roads, parks and public facilities, which can raise property values.
The council plans informational workshops to help residents understand the changes and claim the income tax credit.
Councilwoman Torres promised to revisit the tax structure in two years for assessment and adjustments.
